paragraphs.heading: What cnidarians are
paragraphs.text: Cnidaria is a phylum of more than 11,000 species of invertebrates that live in water, mostly in the sea but also in fresh water. It includes jellyfish, hydroids, sea anemones, corals and some of the tiniest parasites in the sea. The name comes from the Ancient Greek word knídē, meaning "nettle", which recalls the coiled thread of their stinging cells.

paragraphs.heading: Stinging cells
paragraphs.text: What sets cnidarians apart from every other animal is the cnidocyte, a specialized cell that fires a harpoon-like structure. These cells are used mainly to inject venom and catch prey, and in some species they also serve as anchors. They sit on the tentacles that surround the mouth.

paragraphs.heading: Two body forms
paragraphs.text: Most adults take one of two shapes: the medusa, which swims, and the polyp, which stays fixed in one spot. Both are radially symmetrical, the medusa like a wheel and the polyp like a tube, and many hydrozoan species switch between the two. Because they have no head, their ends are named "oral", nearest the mouth, and "aboral", furthest from it. A medusa's jelly is thick and springy, so after the muscles around its edge squeeze water out, it springs back into shape, letting the animal swim by a kind of jet propulsion.

paragraphs.heading: A simple body
paragraphs.text: The body is built from mesoglea, a non-living jelly, sandwiched between two layers of covering cells that are mostly one cell thick. Animals that are more complex have three main cell layers, with no jelly layer between them. A cnidarian has a single opening and body cavity for both digestion and respiration, so it has no separate mouth and anus. A nerve net with no central control, plus simple receptors, keeps its actions in step.

paragraphs.heading: Life cycles
paragraphs.text: Many cnidarian species can reproduce both sexually and asexually. Many have complex life cycles that pass from asexual polyp stages to sexual medusa stages. Some leave out the polyp stage or the medusa stage, and the parasitic classes have evolved to lack both forms.

paragraphs.heading: Hunters and partners
paragraphs.text: Most cnidarians hunt, taking anything from plankton to animals several times their own size. Many, though, get much of their food from symbiotic dinoflagellates, and a few are parasites. Many of the corals that build reefs have polyps packed with symbiotic zooxanthellae that photosynthesize. Reef-building corals keep almost entirely to warm, shallow seas, but other cnidarians live at great depths, in polar regions and in fresh water. They are eaten by starfish, sea slugs, fish, turtles and even other cnidarians.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient line
paragraphs.text: Cnidarians are a very old phylum. Their fossils turn up in rocks about 580 million years old, from the Ediacaran period, before the Cambrian Explosion. Molecular clock studies of mitochondrial genes suggest the group is older still, around 741 million years, earlier than any fossils. Recent studies place cnidarians as the sister group of the bilaterians, which include almost all other animals.
